headline: Canada: daily cannabis use passes daily drinking, CMAJ study finds
dek: A CMAJ study of 99,920 Canadians published on 23 November finds 5.7% use cannabis daily against 5.2% who drink daily, with the gap widest among adults under 35.
key_points: In the 2023-2024 Canadian Community Health Survey, 5.7% of adults reported daily or almost daily cannabis use, against 5.2% for alcohol and 8.5% for cigarettes, the CMAJ paper says.
Daily cannabis use beat daily drinking in every age band from 18 to 49; among women aged 18 to 24 it was 6.6% against 0.4%, about 17.7 times as common.
About 41% of daily consumers started daily use after legalization in October 2018, rising to 85.4% among 18- to 24-year-olds, most of whom were teenagers at the time.
Smoking is still the main way daily consumers take cannabis, and the authors call for marketing and retail limits, higher purchase ages and prevention aimed at frequent use.
body: More adults in Canada now use cannabis every day, or almost every day, than drink alcohol that often. That is the headline finding of a study published on 23 November in the Canadian Medical Association Journal (CMAJ), which compared daily cannabis, alcohol and cigarette use in the provinces using the 2023-2024 Canadian Community Health Survey. Of the 99,920 adults in the analysis, 5.7% reported daily or near-daily cannabis use, compared with 5.2% for alcohol and 8.5% for daily cigarette smoking.

The authors put the number of daily cannabis consumers at about 1.81 million people. The overall gap with alcohol is small, about half a percentage point, but it hides a wide split by age. Daily cannabis use outran daily drinking in every age group from 18 to 49 and outran daily cigarette smoking among adults aged 18 to 34. Among people 65 and older the order flips, and alcohol stays far ahead.
## Who uses cannabis every day

The sharpest numbers are among young adults. Among women aged 18 to 24, 6.6% reported daily cannabis use, against 0.4% who drank daily and 2.0% who smoked cigarettes daily. On the paper's estimate, daily cannabis use in that group was 17.7 times as common as daily drinking, although the confidence interval around that ratio is very wide, running from about 10 to about 68.

The highest single rate by age and sex was among men aged 25 to 34: 10.8% used cannabis daily, compared with 2.9% who drank daily and 8.0% who smoked cigarettes daily. Women of the same age reported 6.8% daily cannabis use, 1.2% daily drinking and 4.5% daily smoking. At the other end of the age range, 3.3% of men and 2.3% of women aged 65 and older used cannabis daily, while 13.0% and 6.7% drank alcohol daily.

The study also looked beyond age. Daily use was reported by 22.6% of respondents who identified as transgender or gender-diverse, 14.7% of people with a mood disorder and 12.2% of people with an anxiety disorder, compared with 4.3% among people without those diagnoses. Daily use fell as income rose, from 7.4% in households earning under C$40,000 to 4.1% above C$150,000. It was much lower among immigrants (1.7%) than among people born in Canada (7.4%). The authors note that some of this use may reflect self-medication or prescribed medical cannabis; the survey did not separate medical from non-medical use.
> The legal market has changed which substance young Canadians use every day. It has not yet changed how most of them use it: they still smoke it.
## Legalization and the smoking question

Two findings bear directly on how Canada's legal market is working. The first is timing. Overall, 41.0% of today's daily consumers said they began daily use after nonmedical cannabis was legalized in October 2018. Among 18- to 24-year-olds the share was 85.4%, but the authors point out that this group was aged 12 to 19 in 2018, the age at which most people start using cannabis whatever the law says. Even among people aged 65 and over, 41.6% started daily use after legalization.

The second is the method. One of the hopes for legalization was that consumers would move from smoking to edibles, beverages and other products. Among daily consumers, 3.9% of all adults mainly smoked cannabis and 1.8% mainly used other methods, so roughly two thirds of daily use is smoked. Of the non-smoking daily consumers, about half (51.9%) mainly vaped, which the authors note is another form of inhalation. In the paper's words, the shift away from smoking may have been limited among the people who use most often.
Daily cannabis use also often stands apart from other daily habits. Only 11.2% of daily cannabis consumers also drank alcohol every day, while 38.4% also smoked cigarettes daily.
## What the researchers want

The study's nine authors are based at McMaster University, the University of Toronto and other Canadian institutions, led by André McDonald, a postdoctoral fellow at McMaster's Peter Boris Centre for Addictions Research. Their conclusion is that screening, treatment and wider policy should give more weight to regular cannabis use, especially among younger adults, people facing social and economic disadvantage, and people with mental health problems.

The paper lists options for regions with established legal markets: stronger risk communication, tighter marketing and retail restrictions, higher minimum purchase ages and prevention aimed at the social and mental health factors behind heavy use. McDonald told the Canadian Press that daily use is strongly associated with cannabis use disorder and that daily smoking exposes users to smoke in ways similar to cigarettes.

Not every expert reads the mental health link the same way. Jibran Khokhar, a Western University addictions researcher who was not involved in the study, told the Canadian Press that whether cannabis causes mental illness or people with mental illness turn to cannabis remains an open question.
## Limits of the data

The authors list several. All answers were self-reported, and stigma may still lead some people to under-report cannabis use. The survey records how often people used a substance, not how much, so a daily cannabis consumer and a pack-a-day smoker are counted the same way. The cannabis and alcohol questions cover the past year while the cigarette question covers the past month. The territories were left out because their data were not yet available, and the survey did not cover nicotine vaping. The authors also caution against comparing these figures directly with other national surveys that use different questions.
The study is also a single snapshot. It shows who uses cannabis daily now; it cannot show whether daily use is still rising.
## What it means for the industry

For Canada's licensed producers and retailers, the paper describes a market whose most frequent buyers are young adults who mainly buy flower and pre-rolls to smoke. That matters because the measures the authors propose, such as marketing limits and a higher purchase age, would land hardest on exactly that customer base. Legal stores sold about C$4.42 billion of cannabis in the first nine months of 2026, as we reported on 21 November, so any policy aimed at frequent use touches a large business.

The research also arrives as other countries study Canada's model. Germany, the United States and others are weighing how far to open commercial sales, and Canadian data on daily use will be cited on both sides of those debates. A separate US study published this month, which we cover in this edition, found that adults with cannabis use disorder had higher odds of serious suicidal thoughts, adding to the evidence base that health regulators are drawing on.
## What to watch

Watch for responses from Health Canada and provincial regulators, which set retail and marketing rules, and for whether any province revisits its minimum purchase age, now 19 in most provinces, 18 in Alberta and 21 in Quebec. The next Canadian Cannabis Survey and the next Canadian Community Health Survey release will show whether daily use is still climbing among adults under 35, and whether the share smoked starts to fall.
